cells.tense: You're here, in the practice, with the pen in your hand.
cells.verb: letting go of what the work is finished with
cells.place: in the room where you repeat a thing until your body knows it
cells.ask: Tend one thing the clearing made room for — give it the same quiet attention you gave the old form, and don't lean on it to hurry. What comes back is this: the letting go keeps arriving on time, as the natural end of something done, not as a loss.
cells.core: You put down what the practice is finished with, when it's finished. Every round through the thing leaves you holding a little less — the tightness in the hand, the method that got you here but won't get you further — and you let it fall without ceremony. That isn't quitting. It's what completion feels like from inside: the work is in your body now, so you no longer have to grip it.
cells.sheetLine: You let go when the thing is done, and it feels like finishing, not losing.

cells.tense: You're already standing at the end you haven't reached yet.
cells.verb: letting go before the work is done
cells.place: in the room where you repeat a thing until your body knows it
cells.ask: Stay for the whole round, one more time, before deciding anything about it — not harder, just all the way to the end, with the door shut and nobody watching. What comes back is the real thing: a letting go that arrives when the work is actually complete, and feels like fulfillment instead of a flinch.
cells.core: You're putting the work down ahead of the finish and calling it surrender. You can already see the version where it doesn't come together, so you release it early — walk out of the hard part with your hands up, generous about it, almost noble — and nobody can accuse you of failing at something you set down on purpose. But the hand hadn't learned it yet. What you're giving up isn't the outcome. It's the repetition that would have made the giving up unnecessary.
cells.sheetLine: You're quitting early and calling it letting go.

cells.tense: You're still at a door the practice already walked through.
cells.verb: unable to let go of what no longer serves
cells.place: in the room where you repeat a thing until your body knows it
cells.ask: Take one thing you carry anyway and carry it with your hands open — the way you'd hold a bird, not a rope — steady, for as long as you'd have gripped it. What comes back is this: the holding gets easier, and the grip you couldn't unclench in the practice starts to loosen on its own, because something is finally finished.
cells.core: You're holding on to a form that already did its work. The method, the old habit of the hand, the way you've always done the rep — it got you somewhere once, and you've kept gripping it long past the point where it was carrying you. That's where the tiredness comes from: not the practice, but the clench around it. Nothing has been released in a long time, so nothing has had room to arrive.
cells.sheetLine: You're exhausted from gripping a practice that's already done its job.

cells.tense: You've put the pen down and you're telling yourself you're still writing — or the other way around.
cells.verb: having already let go without knowing it, or not
cells.place: in the room where you repeat a thing until your body knows it
cells.ask: Look at one thing in the practice and say plainly which it is — still growing in your hands, or already set down — and give whichever is true the care it needs, nothing more. What comes back is this: the letting go becomes something you do on purpose, at the end of something done, instead of something you discover after.
cells.core: Something has already shifted in the practice and the story hasn't caught up. Either the hand has quietly stopped and you're still describing yourself as at it, or you've announced that you've moved on and your body is still showing up every day to do the old thing. One of those is true and you haven't checked which. The release — or the not-release — is already happening. It's just happening without you.
cells.sheetLine: You've either already let go or you haven't — and you haven't looked.
